strengths: Simple, lightweight core idea: replacing a per-image global scale-and-shift with a per-image univariate polynomial transform (whose coefficients are predicted from radar features and MDD depth features) is easy to understand, cheap in parameters (N+1 outputs), and avoids the heavy multi-stage architectures of prior radar–camera fusion pipelines.

Empirical scope is reasonable for the topic: three datasets (nuScenes, ZJU-4DRadarCam, View-of-Delft), three evaluation ranges (50/70/80 m), and four MDD backbones (DPT, Depth Anything, Depth Pro, UniDepth). The backbone study (Tab. 2) shows PolyRad improves over both the raw MDD and the RadarCam-Depth variant for every backbone, which is at least internally consistent evidence that the correction helps regardless of the base estimator.

Component ablations (learnable prototypes, cross-modality attention, monotonicity loss) and a sensitivity study over polynomial degree provide some diagnostic value and show that removing each component degrades MAE, i.e., the design is not entirely arbitrary.

The intuition that monocular metric depth errors are not a single global scale factor is plausible, and a depth-dependent, non-uniform correction is a sensible angle that has received relatively little attention relative to architecture-heavy radar–camera fusion.
weaknesses: Headline numbers are internally inconsistent across the paper. The abstract claims improvements of 30.3% (MAE) and 37.2% (RMSE), the introduction claims 11.3%, 54.6%, 35.2%, and Sec. 4.1 claims 12.1%/10.5% on nuScenes, 46.8%/62.4% on ZJU, and 31.8%/38.5% on VoD. Three mutually incompatible summaries of the same quantity make it impossible to verify the central quantitative claim, and the per-dataset gains derivable from Tab. 1 (e.g., nuScenes ~11% over RadarCam-Depth) do not naturally average to 30.3%/37.2%. This is a material reporting flaw, not a presentation nit.

The paper's core motivation — that linear (scale-and-shift) fitting is insufficient — rests on a suspiciously weak linear baseline. Tab. 3 reports degree-1 fitting at MAE 2156.8 on nuScenes, which is worse than the raw UniDepth prediction (2129.8, Tab. 2) and far worse than the published linear method Lin et al. (1598.2, Tab. 1), and the text even asserts a learned linear fit is worse than deterministic median scaling. A learned scale-and-shift that degrades the input indicates the baseline is mis-specified or under-trained, so the large reported margins over 'linear' may be an artifact rather than evidence of a fundamental limitation of linear transforms.

There is a logical tension between the motivation and the proposed regularizer. The motivation (Fig. 1, Sec. 3.1) is that MDD places several objects at incorrect depths relative to one another and that inflection points fix this, while the loss term L3 = ||1 − dd̂/dz|| pushes the mapping toward a monotone, slope-≈1 transformation that preserves depth ordering. A single global univariate monotone polynomial cannot reorder objects; it can only fix monotone ratio distortions. The paper never reconciles the 'fixes cross-object misalignment' claim with the monotonicity constraint, and the qualitative examples in Fig. 3 (curb vs. asphalt, bus roof vs. distant branch) are more consistent with a systematic, depth-dependent bias than with genuine object-order errors.

The monotonicity regularizer as formulated (Eq. 8–9) is weakly justified: enforcing the average derivative to be close to 1 does not guarantee per-pixel monotonicity (a polynomial with average slope 1 can still oscillate), and the target value of 1 is unit-dependent — z is a scale-less (and, for DPT/Depth Anything, inverted) quantity, so a slope of 1 has no metric meaning. There is no analysis of the relative weights λ1, λ2, λ3 or of how L3 interacts with L1/L2, so the claimed 'principled' constraint is largely heuristic.

Reproducibility is poor. The main paper provides no architecture details (MLP widths/depths, number of prototypes, DCN design), no polynomial degree used for the headline results (Tab. 3 only reports a sensitivity sweep), no training schedule, optimizer, split definitions, or dataset preprocessing beyond the passing references to 'Supp. Mat.', which is not available for assessment. The claimed negligible computational overhead is asserted but never quantified (no runtime, memory, or parameter table). No code release is indicated.

Evaluation is narrow relative to the claims. Only MAE/RMSE at three max-depth caps are reported; there are no δ-threshold accuracies, relative errors, boundary/edge metrics, or any downstream task evaluation (detection, planning, obstacle avoidance), yet the introduction motivates the work by navigation and self-driving. No error bars, seed variance, or significance tests are given, despite the margins at some settings being small.

Dataset-dependent behavior is unexplained and undermines confidence in the protocol. Gains on ZJU (~46–47% MAE) are roughly four times the gains on nuScenes (~10–12%), and the baseline ordering itself changes dramatically across datasets (RadarCam-Depth is far better than other baselines on ZJU yet only marginally better on nuScenes). No analysis is offered for why a single global polynomial would help one dataset so disproportionately, which raises the possibility of dataset-specific bias correction or protocol/split issues rather than a general capability.

The 'degrees of freedom / better-posed system' argument (N+1 polynomial coefficients matched to the cardinality of the radar point cloud) is heuristic and unsubstantiated: the fit is a per-image global function, not a per-point correspondence, and the argument ignores spatial distribution, occlusion, and point quality. Nothing in the paper empirically links radar density or correspondence quality to the achieved error.

Novelty is thin relative to prior art that is cited but not sharply distinguished. Prior works already learn affine/linear or per-image depth transforms guided by additional modalities (e.g., [8], [25], [59], [60]); the incremental contribution here is parameterizing that transform as a low-order polynomial conditioned on radar features. The paper does not clearly position this against concurrent camera-guided scale-resolution methods, and the claim of being 'the first' to frame radar–camera depth as scene fitting is over-broad.
